title: Bitcoin Is Better Money
hook: Your money is broken. Here's why.

sections.title: Why Your Money Loses Value Every Year
sections.content:
Take a dollar bill out of your wallet and look at it. That piece of paper bought a full meal in 1970. Today it barely buys a candy bar. What happened? **Inflation happened.** And it didn't happen by accident — it was engineered.

Every year, the prices of everything you buy creep upward. Your grocery bill gets bigger. Your rent goes up. Gas costs more. But your paycheck? It barely moves. This isn't bad luck or market forces — it's the direct, predictable consequence of how modern money works. Governments and central banks **create new money out of thin air**, and every new dollar they create makes every existing dollar worth a little bit less.

Think of it like this: imagine you're at an auction with 10 people, and everyone has $100. The highest bid for a painting might be $100. Now imagine someone hands 5 of those people an extra $100. The painting doesn't change — but suddenly bids go up to $200. **The painting isn't worth more. The money is worth less.** That's inflation in a nutshell.

Since the Federal Reserve was created in 1913, the US dollar has lost over **96% of its purchasing power**. That means something that cost $1 in 1913 would cost roughly $30 today. Your grandparents aren't exaggerating when they talk about nickel candy bars and penny postcards — the money really was worth that much more.

And the US dollar is actually one of the **better** currencies in the world. In Argentina, the peso has lost 99% of its value in the last 20 years. In Venezuela, the bolivar became so worthless that people literally weighed stacks of bills instead of counting them. Even in Mexico and Brazil, people watch their savings erode year after year as their currencies slowly melt away.

sections.title: The Hidden Tax Nobody Votes For
sections.content:
Here's something your government doesn't want you to think about too carefully: **inflation is a tax.** It's not called a tax. It doesn't show up on your pay stub. No politician has to stand at a podium and vote for it. But it takes money out of your pocket just as surely as income tax does — and it hits the poorest people the hardest.

When the government creates new money to fund its spending, it doesn't need to raise taxes directly. Instead, it dilutes the value of every dollar you already have. If they print 20% more dollars, your savings don't shrink in number — but they shrink in what they can actually buy. You still see the same number in your bank account, but that number buys you less food, less housing, and less of everything else.

**This is the cruelest trick in economics.** Rich people own assets — stocks, real estate, businesses. When new money floods the system, asset prices go up, and rich people get richer. Poor and middle-class people hold their wealth in cash and savings accounts. Their money just sits there, slowly dying. A billionaire with $10 billion in real estate actually **benefits** from inflation because property values rise. A family with $10,000 in savings gets robbed.

The numbers are staggering. If inflation averages just 3% per year — which governments consider perfectly acceptable — your money loses **half its value** in 24 years. That means if you're 30 years old and you put $100,000 in a savings account for retirement, by the time you're 54, it will only buy what $50,000 buys today. You didn't spend it. You didn't lose it. It was **stolen from you by inflation.**

No politician campaigns on the promise of making your savings worth less. But that's exactly what happens every single year, in every country that prints fiat money. It's the tax nobody votes for but everybody pays.

sections.title: How Governments Print Money
sections.content:
When people hear "money printing," they imagine a giant printing press churning out stacks of $100 bills. The reality is both simpler and scarier. **Most new money is created digitally, with a few keystrokes on a computer.**

Here's how it works in the US (and most countries follow a similar playbook). The government wants to spend more money than it collects in taxes — which is basically every year. So the Treasury Department issues bonds (IOUs that promise to pay back the money with interest). Then the Federal Reserve — America's central bank — **buys those bonds by creating brand-new dollars that didn't exist before.** No printing press needed. They just add zeros to a digital account.

This process has a fancy name: **quantitative easing** (QE). But don't let the jargon fool you — it's money printing with extra steps. Between 2020 and 2022, the Federal Reserve created over **$4.6 trillion** in new money. To put that in perspective, that's more than the Fed created in its entire history from 1913 to 2008. In just two years, they printed more money than they had in the previous 95 years combined.

But it gets worse. Banks multiply this new money through something called **fractional reserve banking.** When a bank receives a deposit of $1,000, it only needs to keep a fraction — say $100 — in reserve. It lends out the other $900. That $900 gets deposited somewhere else, and that bank lends out $810 of it. This cycle repeats over and over. By the end, that original $1,000 has turned into roughly $10,000 circulating in the economy. Your money is being diluted not just by the central bank, but by every bank in the system.

In 2020, the Federal Reserve quietly **eliminated reserve requirements entirely.** Banks were no longer required to keep any minimum amount of deposits on hand. Let that sink in: the bank where you keep your savings is not required to actually have your money available. The system runs on trust — and history shows that trust eventually breaks.

sections.title: Bitcoin's Fixed Supply: The Antidote
sections.content:
Now here's where Bitcoin changes everything. **There will only ever be 21 million Bitcoin.** Not 21 million and one. Not 21 million "unless we decide to make more." Exactly 21 million, hard-coded into the software, enforced by mathematics, and verified by every computer on the network.

No president can print more Bitcoin. No central bank can create it with a keystroke. No emergency, no pandemic, no war, no election gives anyone the power to increase the supply. The rules were set in 2009, and they cannot be changed without the agreement of the entire global network — which has never happened and almost certainly never will.

New Bitcoin enters circulation through **mining** — a process where computers compete to solve mathematical puzzles and earn Bitcoin as a reward. But here's the elegant part: the reward gets **cut in half** approximately every four years in an event called the "halving." When Bitcoin started in 2009, miners earned 50 Bitcoin per block. In 2012, it dropped to 25. In 2016, to 12.5. In 2020, to 6.25. In 2024, to 3.125. This will continue until the last fraction of a Bitcoin is mined around the year 2140.

**This is the exact opposite of how dollars work.** The supply of dollars expands constantly and unpredictably — governments can and do create trillions overnight. The supply of Bitcoin expands slowly, predictably, and toward a fixed cap. With dollars, your piece of the pie keeps getting smaller. With Bitcoin, your piece can only stay the same or grow as demand increases against a fixed supply.

Think about what this means for your savings. If you hold dollars, you're guaranteed to lose purchasing power over time. If you hold Bitcoin, you're holding the hardest money ever created — money that cannot be inflated, debased, or diluted by anyone, anywhere, for any reason.

sections.title: Sound Money Throughout History
sections.content:
Bitcoin didn't invent the idea of sound money. For thousands of years, humans have searched for money that holds its value — and the pattern is always the same. **When money is hard to produce, civilizations thrive. When money becomes easy to produce, civilizations collapse.**

The Roman Empire is the classic example. Roman coins were originally made of nearly pure silver. But as the empire expanded and wars got expensive, emperors started **debasing the currency** — mixing in cheaper metals while keeping the face value the same. By the end, Roman "silver" coins contained less than 5% silver. Prices skyrocketed. Trade collapsed. The empire fell. Sound familiar?

Gold became the world's preferred money for a simple reason: **it's hard to produce.** You can't print gold. You can't create it with a computer. You have to dig it out of the ground, which takes enormous effort and expense. This natural scarcity made gold reliable. Societies that used gold as money — from ancient Egypt to the British Empire — experienced relative price stability for centuries.

The gold standard worked beautifully until governments decided it was too inconvenient. In 1971, President Nixon took the US dollar off the gold standard, meaning dollars were no longer backed by physical gold. This freed the government to create as much money as it wanted. Every other country followed suit. **For the first time in 5,000 years of civilization, every currency on Earth was backed by nothing but government promises.**

Since 1971, the purchasing power of the dollar has fallen over 85%. Housing prices have risen 1,500%. The stock market has become a necessity rather than an option, because simply saving money guarantees you'll get poorer. **The entire "invest or die" culture exists because holding cash is a losing strategy in a world of unlimited money printing.**

Bitcoin returns us to the principles of sound money that sustained civilizations for millennia. Like gold, it's scarce and hard to produce. But unlike gold, it's digital, portable, divisible, and verifiable. You can send it anywhere in the world in minutes. You can verify the total supply with your own computer. It's the sound money humanity has been searching for — engineered for the digital age.

sections.title: Why 21 Million Matters
sections.content:
**21 million.** That number is the most important number in the story of money. Here's why.

There are roughly 60 million millionaires in the world. There will only ever be 21 million Bitcoin. **That means there isn't even enough Bitcoin for every millionaire to own one whole coin.** If you own even a fraction of a Bitcoin today, you own something that most wealthy people on Earth will never be able to fully acquire.

The fixed supply creates something economists call **absolute scarcity.** Gold is scarce, but miners discover new deposits every year and mining technology improves over time. The total supply of gold increases by about 1.5% annually. Real estate is scarce, but developers build new properties constantly. Even land can be "created" through reclamation projects. Bitcoin is the first asset in human history with a supply that is **mathematically fixed and completely known in advance.**

Here's what absolute scarcity means for you personally. Every dollar you earn represents your time, your energy, your life force. When you save that dollar, you're storing your life energy for later use. **Inflation steals that stored energy.** It's like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in the bottom — no matter how much you pour in, it keeps draining out. Bitcoin is a bucket with no hole. The energy you pour in stays there.

The 21 million cap also makes Bitcoin the fairest money ever created. **Nobody gets special treatment.** No government can print more for its friends. No central bank can bail out its favored institutions with freshly created coins. No insider can get early access to new supply. Everyone plays by the same rules, and those rules can't be changed. A teenager in El Salvador and a hedge fund manager in New York have the exact same monetary guarantees.

Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin's anonymous creator, chose 21 million for practical reasons — it works well with the halving schedule and allows for enough divisibility (each Bitcoin can be divided into 100 million units called satoshis). But the philosophical significance goes far deeper. By creating money with a fixed supply, Satoshi gave humanity something it has never had: **money that is truly, permanently, uncompromisingly scarce.** And that changes everything.
